text: Cassini had spent years flying around Saturn and hanging close to Enceladus and Titan, so it was basically a possible contaminant if it ended up stuck orbiting a moon. The worry was that a small fault could leave it there, and then a crash would bring Earth microbes and hardware bits onto a place scientists still thought might be habitable. So the Grand Finale put it on a path straight into the atmosphere. Falling into Saturn's gas was the safer bet. I'd pick that too, rather than risk a moon hit. That way any debris just sinks into Saturn's gas.

Yeah, the “stationary” leg hurts because it isn't really just standing there. Every push is a small sprint: your pushing leg bends deep at the hip, knee, and ankle, and that same leg has to absorb impact when you turn or land from a small hop. If you're a beginner, those muscles aren't used to it, so they ache the way any untrained muscle would after repeated work. I've always figured a lot of people blame the standing leg, but the strain often comes from pushing and recovery, not from simply balancing.

If you lock your knee on the stationary leg to make it seem steady, the joint takes a sharp load instead of letting the muscles absorb it. That can make the knee or hip hurt more, especially if you're also pushing off hard. Skateboards make you shift weight a lot: one leg braces, the other pushes, then you recover. That back-and-forth means the non-pushing side is doing more work than it looks like. It's the same reason a runner's non-kicking leg can be sore after long runs; it's part of the cycle, not a broken part. I'd check your foot angle and board width too. If the board is too narrow or too long, the stationary leg gets twisted to hold balance, which isn't a natural line for the hip.

So if it's dull and spread out, it's likely muscle fatigue. If it's sharp in the knee, hip, or ankle, slow down, check your stance, and don't ride through pain that makes your form get weird. A few minutes of hip and ankle mobility before you ride, and a short walk afterward, usually helps. But don't invent a medical diagnosis; if the pain lingers or changes how you stand, get someone to look at it.

You're right that most Black Americans aren't from Africa today. The name isn't about where someone is living, it's about where part of their ancestry came from. For a lot of people, that means West or Central Africa, even if their families had been in the US for generations. The slave trade moved millions of people from the continent, and later, especially after 1950, more Africans also came directly to the US, so 'African' in the name can mean either the ancestral connection or a recent immigrant connection. I wouldn't read it as a birthplace claim. If you say Afro-American, you're naming an ethnic identity built around African roots, not saying every person's passport is from Lagos or Kinshasa. Some people prefer Black American, others African American, and some use other terms, but the prefix points to the historical tie, not to a current address. That's the part that trips people up: ancestry is not the same thing as citizenship or residence. So the name is a broad marker of origin and cultural lineage, and it doesn't require the person to have been born on the continent. It's a bit like calling someone of Irish descent 'Irish-American'; the name signals heritage, not a recent visa.

Mostly from government shipments, often Russian or Iranian, captured stockpiles, border smuggling, and local black markets. In a town you can walk into an arms bazaar and buy a rifle, bullets, or a machine gun, or a relative can pull a stash out from under the floor. They keep getting them because the fighting never fully stopped. A gun is how you protect your street, your house, or your faction's piece of territory; even after the government took Damascus, local groups still need guns to keep others off their backs. And nobody trusts the ceasefire enough to throw their guns away.

If you mean all medications, that's not really true; caffeine and aspirin are drugs, and they are widely used with manageable effects. The issue is mostly the recreational ones that make you feel euphoric. There isn't really a class of drug that gives a strong high and leaves zero downside, because the same brain systems that make the pleasure can also get used to it. Take cocaine: it blocks dopamine from being recycled, so more dopamine stays active and you feel wired and happy. But the brain responds by lowering its own dopamine signaling, and after repeated use you need more for the same effect. That's not just a bad habit, it's the body trying to keep things in check. With opioids like heroin or morphine, the effect comes through opioid receptors, and the body reduces that receptor sensitivity too. So tolerance builds, withdrawal hurts, and the margin between a good dose and a bad one can be thin. Alcohol is even more variable because it hits multiple systems and can change how your heart, breathing and judgement work. The 0 adverse effects idea runs into a basic problem: if a drug strongly activates the reward pathways, homeostasis pushes back, and if it doesn't, you're not getting the intense euphoria you're asking for. Even mild stimulants have a downside; they can disturb sleep, appetite, anxiety, and blood pressure. There are drugs with fewer side effects, but they're not the intense euphoric ones you named. Even if you pick a drug that seems safe at first, the dose that gives you the strong effect is not the same for everyone. A drug can treat a problem, but that doesn't mean a strong euphoric one will leave you unchanged after repeated use. My guess is that a truly zero-adverse-effect strong high is close to impossible, because pleasure and side effect come from the same neurochemical mess. You can design a drug to be gentler, but you can't get the strong reward without the body noticing and adapting. So the practical answer is not that every drug is bad, but that the powerful mood-altering ones carry a real cost: tolerance, withdrawal, individual reaction, and risk of taking too much. For this person, I'd say the fear is reasonable, but '0 adverse effects' is too strong a claim to expect from anything that hits the reward system hard. You can live with some downsides, but you probably can't get away with none.

Hi,

I get it, it's not just in your head. If your head starts aching while you're out with your wife, I'd guess it's the mix of standing around, small talk, and the heat of the store. A long day in malls is a low-grade endurance test: poor air, constant small movements, and the stress of keeping up. It's not a migraine, because it's tied to the situation, not the usual tension headache pattern. Try to pace with her, get air more often, and don't treat it as a puzzle to solve on the spot. And have a drink.

Thanks

Hi,

When he made you say "silk" five times and spell it, your mind was probably stuck on the exercise. By the time he asked about cows, "milk" just came out because it's the word you associate with a cow, not the thing they drink. That doesn't mean you're weird. You answered the cow question with the strongest mental link.

I think he was using that first part to see if you'd repeat what you'd been told. Some people do those kinds of checks, maybe to see if you're following directions, or if you mix up simple facts.

I wouldn't make a big deal of it. If you feel like the milk answer slipped out, it's more about what your brain grabbed onto, not proof of anything bad. If it keeps happening, you could ask him why he did that; he might explain what he's trying to test.

Thanks

Hi,

I'll try to help where I can, but take my words with a grain of salt. I've been through the process once, and a few things stuck with me.

The survey matters more than the photos, so ask for it before you commit. I'd also get the mortgage in principle early; it saves the back and forth when you finally find something.

Your friend's mention of the silk/milk thing? That's just a local story; I wouldn't let it drive the decision. Check what's actually going on at the street level. Are the neighbours pleasant, is there parking, and does the plumbing look sound. Those small things ruin the fun later if you skip them.

Budget hard. You know the trap: you see a house you like, and then spend the money you were keeping for furniture, carpets, and all the little things. I'd keep at least 10% of the purchase price in reserve, because the moving day surprises are not funny.

And whatever you do, don't get swayed by the estate agent. Their job is to sell, not to save your money.

Thanks

Mike

Hi,
I figured you wanted the straight version. A 3-in-1 is one formula trying to cover three jobs, washing your body, cleansing hair, and leaving hair with a bit of condition. That means it has to be gentle enough for skin and still carry some conditioning stuff, which is where it differs from a normal bodywash or a 2-in-1 shampoo/conditioner. Compared with separate products, it is a compromise. It isn't going to lather or scrub like a dedicated bodywash, and it won't give the same clean on hair as a proper shampoo. The conditioning part is usually just enough to reduce tangles, not the full treatment of a real conditioner. Against a 2-in-1, the extra bit is that it's also meant for skin, so you can wash your whole body in one go. In practice, that convenience often comes at a cost: it may feel so mild that you might use more product or wash twice. It's the kind of thing you reach for when you don't want to juggle bottles. My take is that it is handy for travel or lazy mornings, but if your hair or skin is picky, separate products will still do their jobs better.
Thanks

Hi,

You asked how people measure continental speed, so here is the plain version. They don't time a continent crossing a map in one sitting. They set up permanent GPS stations on the crust and take repeated position fixes. The difference between fixes, divided by elapsed time, gives a velocity. Most modern plates are tracked this way; the stations are placed so their motion represents the plate, not just local ground effects.

The velocities come out in millimetres per year, which feels tiny until you think about it over thousands of years. GPS can resolve those tiny changes when the station is stable and the data are compared against a reference frame. If a station sits near a fault or on shifting ground, its local motion can be off, so networks use many stations and average out the noise. Older methods used sea-floor spreading, but GPS is the workhorse now. This is how plate speeds are pulled from routine survey work. So the answer is: repeated GPS positions on land, not one measurement, and the math is just change in position over time.

That should settle it for you. Let me know if you want the details on reference frames or the older spreading evidence.

Thanks

Inbreeding does not make genes worse; it raises the chance that two identical copies of a harmful allele appear in the same child. Many small genetic effects influence cognitive ability, and most are hidden in the general population because harmful copies are kept apart. When relatives mate, the shared ancestry makes it more likely that both parents carry the same rare variant, so the child can inherit two copies. That increased homozygosity can expose recessive defects, and for traits like IQ the combined effect tends to pull scores below the average of the wider population.

This is an average statistical pattern, not a guarantee. A child of inbreeding can still have an average or high IQ, while another may be below average. The science here is basic Mendelian inheritance plus population genetics: inbreeding increases homozygosity, which makes rare harmful alleles express themselves more often in a measurable way.

An injury to the arm can feel less bad than, say, the same blow to the face, ribs, or foot. The arm is more padded and further from the core, so the body treats it as less threatening. Pain is not just tissue damage; the brain also weighs location, how much of your day depends on that body part, and whether you can still move. If you can use the arm for typing or carrying things, even for work that needs both hands, the signal may be downgraded.

That does not mean the arm is easy to hit, because the brachial plexus and bones can make it sharp or numb. For a wiki page, put it simply: location matters, attention matters, and "less hurt" is often a perception, not proof the injury is mild. New hires should still report pain honestly, rather than assuming arm pain is just a scratch.

Carbon monoxide (CO) is nasty because it binds to the haemoglobin in your blood about 200 times more strongly than oxygen. Once it's there, your blood struggles to carry oxygen to your organs. CO is colourless and odourless, so you often don't notice it until you feel dizzy or sick.

CO2 isn't that tricky at the levels we normally breathe. Your body constantly makes it, and the lungs get rid of it as you breathe out. At everyday concentrations, it's manageable. It does become hazardous when the air is badly depleted or when CO2 builds up in a sealed space, but that's not the usual office or home situation.

One more practical point: CO doesn't just make oxygen hard to pick up; it also makes it hard for haemoglobin to let oxygen go where the tissue needs it. That means symptoms can creep up quietly, especially if you're sleeping. A little CO can build up while you can't sense it, which is why detectors are useful in places with gas stoves, heaters, or enclosed garages.

If it were me explaining it to a new colleague, I'd keep it to this: oxygen and CO both need haemoglobin. CO wins that competition by a huge margin. Carbon dioxide (CO2) is mostly a waste gas the body is built to clear. The difference is not that CO2 is completely harmless. It's that CO can do damage at concentrations where CO2 feels fine.

So if you're working in a hot, enclosed room with a heater or running engine nearby, treat a dull headache, nausea, or unexplained tiredness as a signal. CO poisoning is one of those things where a small detector is cheap insurance. You don't need to be a chemist to see why this matters. The gas is quiet, and the body doesn't warn you early.

If an aircraft hits something, your body keeps moving at the speed you were already travelling. The brace position is how you stop that motion in a controlled way, so your head and chest absorb the impact rather than slamming into a tray table or seat in front of you. The main idea is to lower yourself and protect your most vulnerable parts. You lean forward, keep your head down or against the seat in front, and put your hands over your face or mouth, with feet flat on the floor. It's less about being comfortable and more about keeping your airway and head protected while your feet stay planted. That posture reduces the chance of your head hitting the seat frame, and it keeps you more likely to stay in the seat. It also helps you remain conscious if the floor jolts you, which matters because an unconscious person is much harder to move. The position is not perfect, and different aircraft use slightly different versions, but the goal is the same: turn a hard stop into something your body can handle. In an emergency you follow the crew's instruction and hold the brace until they say it's safe to move.

Before the industrial era, most businesses were small, family-run workshops and their names did not need to be famous beyond their town. When ownership changed hands or a shop closed, the business often ended with the person, so few old names carried on unchanged.

The few that survived usually kept a label while the actual company was rebuilt, renamed, or bought out by later players. That is why you may see old names in shops or trademarks, but the company behind them is usually a newer organization using an old brand rather than a business that ran since before factories.

I still think the bank won out because the dealership's low rate came with hidden padding. I wasn't trying to be clever, just checking the fine print, and it was there in black and white. The dealer was offering a lower nominal rate, but they also added a document fee, a paint protection package, and rolled an extra amount into the loan. My bank's quote was a plain loan, no bundled products. The bank's rate was higher, but the balance was smaller and there were no surprise add-ons. When you multiply the monthly payment by the number of months and add the fees, the bank was cheaper.

Here's a quick way to see it. Say the car is $30,000 and the dealer offers 4% over 60 months, plus a $750 doc fee and a $1,200 protection package. The lower rate doesn't help if the loan balance is padded and you're paying interest on money you didn't need to borrow. The bank at 6% on the same $30,000, with no extras, can end up costing less in total. You're paying a higher rate, but on a smaller balance and without the padding. The dealer's low rate is a marketing trick; the real cost shows up in the add-ons.

The difference isn't magic. A lower interest rate only saves money if the rest of the loan is the same size. Dealers earn from add-ons and fees, so they can advertise the low rate while the invoice gets longer. If the dealer's loan is inflated, the rate cut may be smaller than the extra interest you pay on the inflated balance. My bank quote was just the car price and the loan, with a separate fee line. That makes comparison much easier. I've seen this in practice: the dealer's rate looked better, but the final amount due was higher once the protection and doc fees were included.

I get why people fall for it. The dealer's sign says lower rate, and that catches the eye. But the bank's quote is plainer. I'd always run the total. Multiply the payment by the term, add the fees, compare with the bank. If the dealer's package is optional but recommended, that's how the extra revenue happens. The bank doesn't have to sell you extras, so its number is easier to trust. The trick is simple. Compare the total out-the-door cost, not just the headline rate.

I’m still not convinced marijuana should be legal in every single US state, but I do think the current patchwork makes sense if it’s handled carefully. Right now you can buy it at a licensed store in one state and get stopped at a checkpoint in the next, and that gap between medical and adult-use laws is where people get into trouble. I don’t blame states for moving slowly; each has to decide whether it wants tax revenue, and which license rules to use. Some states have separate rules for who can apply, what they can sell, and where stores may open. For me in practice the sensible path is medical first, adult use second, and federal rules that don’t punish a state just because it legalized. Until that happens, people should know their home state, their destination, and whether the product came from a licensed shop or somebody’s garden.

I've always figured our bodies are more like batteries than little lightning rods. The electricity in us comes from tiny voltage differences across cell membranes. Sodium and potassium ions pump in and out of nerve and muscle cells. When a nerve fires, channels open and sodium rushes in, flipping the membrane charge for a split second. That quick flip is an action potential. In my heart, the same ion movement starts in the SA node and spreads through the chambers, which is why an ECG can show it as a jagged line. It isn't sparks; it's controlled ion flow.

Sampling an old song is less like copying a song and more like borrowing a voice from somewhere else. If I were starting from a record I like, I'd find a clean rip, not a radio edit. I keep a folder of source audio, and the first thing I check is whether the track is in the key I need. If it's a half step off, I don't force it; I pick another cut. The old recording doesn't have to be perfect. A little hiss, a bit of warble, can be part of the texture.

The process is hands-on. I load the sample into a DAW, then trim the part I want, maybe a two-bar phrase or a drum break. Then I chop it into smaller pieces and lay them under the new song. I might pitch it up or down a half step, time-stretch it to my beat, and add a little reverb so it sits in the mix. If I'm using a vocal, I try to pull the voice out of the mix without leaving too much bass rumble. I don't chase perfection here; I just want the old fragment to feel like it belongs in the new arrangement.

Permission is where a lot of people get stuck. You can make something great, but if you plan to release it, you need to clear the sample. That can mean writing to the original owner or using a service. I've seen producers skip this and lose a song they loved. It's a bit unfair that a few seconds of audio can make a release feel legally risky.

There's a temptation to over-sample a track until it loses its own identity. My position is simple: use just enough of the old song to make a point. One sharp phrase can do more work than a wall of chopped loops. I'd rather leave the listener with one recognizable fragment than drown them in layers. The best samples I've heard don't shout; they sit quietly under the new composition and give it history.

I think the question isn't really about technique only. Sampling older songs is a way of letting old music keep moving through new work. You're not erasing where it came from. You're giving it another life, and if you do that respectfully, the sample becomes a bridge between the two songs. That's why I still reach for an old recording even when I could make the sound from scratch.

When I get a headache, the first thing I want to know is why my head hurts. My take is simple: your brain itself doesn't really feel pain, so the hurt comes from the stuff wrapped around it. The membranes, blood vessels, sinuses, neck muscles, and nerves are the parts that can be irritable. When something sets them off, they send pain signals up through the trigeminal and other nerves, and the brain reads that as a throb or tight band. For me, it feels like pressure behind the eyes and a squeeze across the forehead, sometimes with a dull ache in the back of the neck. I've always figured headaches are the body's alarm, not proof of damage. The detail that matters is that pain is an interpretation, not a tiny injury in the brain. It's less a mystery and more a pattern you can notice, if you keep track of when it starts.

We couldn't even tell if the food is good, because we never got to eat. We got there at 7:20 p.m. on Sunday, picked this place on purpose since we had a 10:00 p.m. show at the same hotel and thought it'd be easy. We put our names on their completely useless digital waitlist, and they told us to come back and pay at 8:23. We did, but stood there until 8:40 before a staff member casually said we probably wouldn't be seated until 9:15. It was only two of us, and they offered no fix. If the wait runs that far past payment, tell people upfront so their night isn't totally wasted. Absolute disaster. Zero stars would really be my personal choice.

I went to this buffet on a Friday around 4:30 p.m., and, surprisingly, there was no line at all. For two of us, the total bill came out to about $130, which felt pretty steep. Before going, I'd figured the price would be comparable to a steakhouse. Afterward, I learned the buffet actually cost somewhat more than what I'd expected to pay.

I was disappointed that steak wasn't on the menu at all. At that price, I'd assumed there'd be some kind of steak option. The meat choices included lamb, prime rib, and chicken, but those are things you can find at other Las Vegas buffets for much less money.

The seafood station had Alaskan crab legs and rock crab claws. Alaskan crab legs are available at a lot of Vegas buffets, but I hadn't run into rock crab claws anywhere else, so those were genuinely interesting. The problem was there were no crab-claw crackers. Staff said wooden mallets were available, but our table was so close to the next table that I didn't really want to start smashing crab shells and send pieces flying at the people next to us. So I just ate the crab legs.

The Asian station didn't seem especially distinctive either. It reminded me quite a bit of the buffet at Rampart Casino. Dessert had gelato and pastries, but nothing really stood out. They also had fresh juices, although I didn't try any.

I'd call the buffet acceptable, but overpriced for what it offers. If you're curious, it's worth trying once, especially if there's no wait. But if the line is long, I'd probably reconsider.

★★★★☆ Keeping it

The space bar rattles. Hit it with the edge of your thumb and it sounds like a loose pen cap in a drawer. The E key also repeats now and then, so "example" becomes "eexample" and I have to backspace. It happens maybe once an afternoon, always when I'm typing fast and not looking.

I paid $38 and kept it anyway, because of the switches. When I asked the seller what they were, the answer took a week. By then I had already pulled off a keycap and found out for myself: brown tactile switches, with a small bump under the finger and a soft landing at the bottom. My old membrane board felt like pressing wet cardboard by comparison.

My job is mostly email, often two or three hours in a row, and my wrists don't ache by the end anymore. That mattered more than the rattle.

Sending it back would have meant paying for postage and boxing it up, and I'd have been without a keyboard while I waited. So it stays on the desk, and I tap the space bar a little bit closer to the middle now.

I've gone to Vegas pretty much my whole life, well, the under-21 version of it, so I've sat through a lot of shows before I could even gamble. Le Rêve at the Wynn is one I finally caught, and mixed, maybe slightly worse than mixed. The circular stage is genuinely smart. You're basically looking down into it, so from almost any seat you get a really decent view, which is rare in Vegas. Some individual acts are impressive too, strength stuff, aerialists, divers. Those people are athletes, no question. But a lot of it reminded me of Cirque du Soleil. Not in a rip-off way exactly, if you've seen Cirque, you've seen comparable feats, maybe with more clarity.

And clarity is the problem. What's the story? I still don't know. There's a dream, maybe? A guy? Water? It felt like a bunch of pretty images thrown at you, and the show never tells you what it's trying to say. Also there's way too much happening at once. Too many people, too many elements, too many wow moments stacked on top of each other. A more restrained production would hit harder. This felt like that stereotypical Vegas spectacle thing where more must be better, so they crammed everything in.

Ticket note: if you're staying at Wynn or Encore, they have a deal, $99 instead of the normal $125. That helps. Would I see it again? Probably not, and I wouldn't pay for it a second time. Apart from a few stunts, it was just average. I wasn't really blown away, and I don't think anyone else was really either. That said, a few friends liked it, and if you've never seen it, maybe check it out. Just don't expect to leave overwhelmed.

About two years ago, we ordered two shirts for my father by phone from Rockmount Ranch Wear. The sales rep wrote our delivery address wrong: her handwritten “7” was read as a “1.” We gave 5407, but the package went to 5401. The residents there brought it to the local UPS store for return. Then the package disappeared, and it was never seen or heard from again. We didn’t learn until several weeks later. While the dispute was going on, we placed an additional order for two more shirts. Rockmount refused to refund the original two. At that stage the owner handled it. He acknowledged the shipment went to the wrong address, but said no refund until the shirts were returned. He claimed we were partly responsible because we hadn’t been friendly enough with the residents at 5401, four doors away. We disputed the original charge with our credit card company and in the end we eventually got a credit.
